query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: By integrating high-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) with in-situ calibrated dilatometry, one can accurately determine the melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting for high-entropy alloys, achieving measurement precisions of ±5 K for Tm and ±5–10% for enthalpic and entropic parameters across a range of HEA compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic high-entropy alloys (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) in well-prepared, miniature sample forms ensuring uniform temperature distribution.
generation.intervention: Conducting atmosphere-controlled DSC experiments using optimized heating and cooling rates (e.g., 5–50 K/min) integrated with in-situ dilatometry to capture volumetric changes at the phase transition.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under an inert (e.g., argon) atmosphere with precise temperature control and automated sample handling to enable high throughput; high-temperature in-situ calibration routines are implemented using reference materials.
generation.structural_mediator: The clear thermal signatures (endothermic/exothermic peaks) during the phase transition in DSC data, alongside simultaneous dilatometric signals reflecting volumetric changes, serve as the mediators.
generation.mechanism: The DSC measures the heat flow during melting and solidification, allowing extraction of melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy, while the integrated dilatometry, once rigorously calibrated at high temperatures, tracks volume changes. Together, these datasets allow for precise determination of liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperature measurements with an accuracy of ±5 K, and enthalpy/entropy and volume change determinations within an uncertainty range of ±5–10%; the approach is expected to be efficient for screening various HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Standard DSC measurements on simpler alloy systems demonstrating similar accuracies, coupled with prior studies using differential thermal analysis as referenced (e.g., PMC7412006).
generation.boundary: The method is most applicable to HEAs with similar melting characteristics and may require further adaptation for alloys with exceptionally high melting points or unconventional phase transition kinetics.
generation.uncertainty: Sources of uncertainty include potential calibration drift at high temperatures, integration of dilatometry under rapid thermal changes, and sample heterogeneities; these uncertainties are mitigated through rigorous in-situ calibration using established high-temperature reference points.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform experiments on well-characterized reference alloys with established melting temperatures, enthalpy, and volume change values using the combined DSC/dilatometry setup. Compare the measured values with literature benchmarks.
measurements: Integrated latent heat from the heat flow curve
Volume change as determined by dilatometry calibrated against high-temperature standards
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If measured melting temperatures deviate by more than ±5 K or enthalpy/volume change values deviate by more than ±10% from the literature values for the reference alloys, the proposed integrated DSC/dilatometry approach is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Differential thermal analysis was performed with a Setaram Setsys 2400 instrument modified to enable excursions to 2500 °C. The experiments were conducted in Ar flow at heating and cooling rates 20 °C/min using WRe differential heat flow sensor and thermocouple for furnace temperature control. Laser-melted beads, 100–140 mg in weight were placed in tungsten crucibles and sealed under Ar atmosphere to avoid the possibility of sample and standards contamination with carbon vapor from vitreous carbon protection tube. Multiple measurements were performed on each sample. Temperatures of phase transformations were determined as average from the onset [] of endothermic peaks on heating. Enthalpies of phase transformation were calculated as the averages of absolute values of endothermic heat effects on heating and exothermic heat effects on cooling. The instrument and methodology were described in detail elsewhere [,,,]. Temperature and sensitivity calibrations were performed using melting and phase transition temperatures and enthalpies of Au (1064 °C), Al2O3 (2054 °C), Nd2O3 (A-H, H-X, and X-L at 2077, 2201 and 2308 °C, respectively), and Y2O3 (C-H and H-L at 2348 °C and 2439 °C, respect

The temperature dependent molar heat capacity cp(T) of the specimen was experimentally determined in alumina crucibles using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC 204, Netzsch, Selb, Germany) in the temperature range from −170 °C to 600 °C under a flushing flow of nitrogen. In this temperature range oxidation of the samples is not critical. For T = 20 °C − TS (if TS < 1600 °C) samples were measured using a Netzsch DSC 404 F1 Pegasus under an Ar 5.0 gas flush with a rate of 70 ml/min in crucibles composed of 80% Pt and 20% Rh. The crucibles are lined with ceramic inlays to prevent interaction of the metallic specimens with the Pt-Rh crucible. The calibration of temperature and enthalpy of the two Netzsch devices was performed using the calibration set 6.239.2–91.3 under the conditions of 10 K/min and a nitrogen flow of 40 mL/min. The two measurements were evaluated for each material and the curves were connected in the common temperature range from room temperature to 600 °C.

proposals.intervention: High-throughput differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) with optimized heating/cooling rates
proposals.conditions: Atmosphere-controlled DSC experiments performed over a range of heating rates (e.g., 5–50 K/min) on miniature samples to ensure uniform temperature distribution
proposals.structural_mediator: Phase transition signature as observed by the endothermic/exothermic peaks associated with melting and solidification
proposals.mechanism: The DSC measures the heat flow associated with melting, allowing extraction of melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy of fusion; by calibrating volumetric changes via complementary dilatometry integrated into the DSC setup, one can also deduce the volume change at melting, and, with further calibration, estimate liquid-phase thermodynamic properties
proposals.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of Tm within ±5 K, enthalpy and entropy within ±5%, and volume change with similar precision; efficient screening across various HEA compositions due to sample miniaturization and automation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This method directly measures the thermal response during phase transitions, offering a high-throughput, reliable approach that applies to the diverse family of HEAs. Its quantitative performance specifications are clear, and it builds on established DSC technology which has been successfully applied to simpler alloy systems.

proposals.material_system: Representative HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) simulated by atomistic models
proposals.intervention: First-principles molecular dynamics (FPMD) combined with thermodynamic integration methods
proposals.conditions: Simulations performed under constant pressure (NPT ensemble) across a temperature range spanning below and above the expected melting point; simulations of systems containing several hundred atoms over tens of picoseconds
proposals.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder transition from solid to liquid as captured by pair distribution functions and diffusion coefficients
proposals.mechanism: FPMD simulations capture the evolution of interatomic interactions and structural changes at melting. Thermodynamic integration allows accurate computation of free energy differences between solid and liquid phases, from which melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change upon fusion can be deduced. Liquid-phase properties are extracted from equilibrium simulations of the molten state.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Predictions of melting temperature within ±10 K, enthalpy and entropy within ±10% relative to experimental benchmarks, and detailed atomic-level insights into melting phenomena; applicable across a wide range of HEA compositions by adjusting simulation parameters
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This computational approach provides a complementary, highly controllable method to determine melting and fusion properties across the HEAs. It extends the understanding of physical mechanisms at an atomic scale and can be efficiently applied to screen materials, providing predictions that can be directly compared with experiments.

proposals.material_system: High-entropy alloys processed via containerless methods (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi, AlCoCrFeNi)
proposals.intervention: Electromagnetic levitation (EML) combined with in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and high-speed video imaging
proposals.conditions: Experiments conducted under high vacuum or inert gas, with sample heating achieved by EML to avoid container contamination, and in-situ XRD performed during controlled heating and cooling cycles
proposals.structural_mediator: Real-time observation of structural evolution and density changes in the sample as it transitions from the solid to the liquid state
proposals.mechanism: EML enables contamination-free heating and accurate control of thermal gradients. In-situ XRD captures the onset of melting and structural disorder, while high-speed video and radiography track volumetric changes. Combined data analysis yields melting temperature, latent heat (from integration with known specific heat data), and liquid-phase densities that inform the estimation of enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of melting temperature within ±5 K, and validation of volume change and enthalpic contributions to within ±5–10% uncertainty; successful application across a range of high-entropy alloys with different compositions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach addresses both the precision and efficiency requirements by leveraging containerless processing to avoid sample contamination and in-situ synchrotron diagnostics to capture transient phenomena during melting; it extends current experimental techniques and provides decisive results that can rule out models if discrepancies arise in the structural data.

proposals.material_system: Broad range of HEAs, including equiatomic and non-equiatomic systems (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi, AlxCoCrFeNi)
proposals.intervention: Laser-melting combined with ultrafast time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy
proposals.conditions: Laser pulses (with pulse durations in the nanosecond to microsecond range) are used to locally melt samples under inert atmosphere, while time-resolved X-ray absorption monitors the evolution of the local atomic structure, with measurements taken at sub-millisecond intervals
proposals.structural_mediator: Temporal evolution of the local atomic coordination environment, as the signature of the transition from ordered solid to disordered liquid
proposals.mechanism: The rapid heating and subsequent cooling induced by pulsed laser melting minimizes diffusion and allows the capture of dynamic melting events. Ultrafast X-ray absorption spectroscopy provides an element-specific probe of the electronic and geometric structure near the melting point. Analysis of the transient spectra, in conjunction with energy balance calculations, can yield precise values of Tm, the latent heat (from the integrated energy change), and derived thermodynamic properties for the liquid phase.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Determination of melting temperature within ±5 K, latent heat and entropy changes with a precision better than ±10%, and resolved transient volume changes; highly applicable to HEAs with complex chemistries over a wide compositional range
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This method emphasizes efficiency and accuracy by capturing the melting process in real-time, giving a direct measure of phase-transition thermodynamics before extensive post-processing effects can interfere. A decisive validation result would be the inability of the time-resolved spectra to detect a consistent phase transition signature, which would rule out the approach.

critiques.addresses_problem: Directly measures the phase-transition thermal effects, extracting melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy, and via complementary dilatometry the volume change at melting. This directly targets the question's properties.
critiques.constraints: It specifically targets equiatomic HEAs like CoCrFeMnNi and utilizes controlled atmosphere DSC experiments on miniature samples, which respects the material system and experimental constraints.
critiques.physical_soundness: The physical principle is well‐established; DSC measures heat flow during transitions and dilatometry tracks volume changes. Hence, the mechanism is sound in this specific regime.
critiques.feasibility: High-throughput DSC combined with calibrated dilatometry is an established method and is feasible with current instrumentation, provided high-temperature calibrations are maintained.
critiques.evidence: Prior studies have successfully used differential thermal analysis and DSC on alloy systems (e.g., PMC7412006, PMC7513177, PMC9325168).
critiques.main_risk: The integration of dilatometry into the DSC setup and ensuring precise calibration at the high temperatures relevant for HEAs may be challenging.
critiques.fix: Implement rigorous, in-situ calibration routines with high-temperature reference materials to ensure both DSC and dilatometric data remain accurate.

critiques.addresses_problem: Offers a real‐time probe of the melting event via ultrafast X-ray absorption spectroscopy, which can capture transient atomic reconfigurations and determine melting temperature, latent heat, and liquid-phase properties.
critiques.constraints: It is designed to be applicable across a broad range of HEAs, including non-equiatomic systems, and operates under inert atmosphere using pulsed laser melting. However, the rapid heating may not fully suit equilibrium measurements required by some thermodynamic parameters.
critiques.physical_soundness: The combination of laser melting with time-resolved XAS is physically sound for capturing dynamic structural evolution; however, the extremely fast transient may introduce non-equilibrium effects.
critiques.feasibility: While ultrafast XAS is available at synchrotron facilities, the experimental setup is complex and requires high synchronization between laser pulses and X-ray probes.
critiques.evidence: Evidence exists for time-resolved studies of phase transitions and atomic ordering processes (e.g., PMC11294451, PMC11935079, PMC6207727, PMC4652022), though not all directly on HEA melting.
critiques.main_risk: The transient nature of laser-induced melting may lead to non-equilibrium conditions that could distort thermodynamic measurements.
critiques.fix: Introduce intermediate equilibrium validation steps or adjust pulse parameters to slow down the melting progression, ensuring that the measured properties reflect near-equilibrium thermodynamics.

critiques.addresses_problem: Uses first-principles molecular dynamics combined with thermodynamic integration to compute melting-related properties, directly addressing the question from an atomic-scale perspective.
critiques.constraints: Focused on representative HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with simulation parameters tailored to capture phase transitions, although simulation length and size may impose restrictions on the range of HEAs accurately modeled.
critiques.physical_soundness: The approach is based on well-established electronic structure methods and thermodynamic integration, making it physically sound, albeit with limitations in time and system size.
critiques.feasibility: FPMD simulations for hundreds of atoms over picosecond timescales are feasible, but require significant computational resources and might not capture slow kinetics or subtle long-range effects in complex HEAs.
critiques.evidence: Supporting literature using AIMD and combined atomistic simulation techniques (e.g., PMC8282813, PMC9435032, PMC8746459, PMC8950179) indicates the viability of such computational methods though often with limited quantitative precision.
critiques.main_risk: The limited system sizes and simulation time scales may result in inaccuracies in predicting melting parameters for complex HEAs.
critiques.fix: Extend simulation durations and increase supercell sizes, or incorporate enhanced sampling techniques to better capture the thermodynamics of melting in HEAs.

critiques.addresses_problem: Determines melting temperature and related thermodynamic properties via in-situ observation of structural changes and density variations using electromagnetic levitation combined with synchrotron XRD and high-speed imaging.
critiques.constraints: It is well-suited for HEAs processed containerlessly (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi, AlCoCrFeNi) and minimizes contamination, thereby respecting the operating conditions and material constraints outlined.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; containerless processing avoids contamination while real-time XRD and imaging capture the phase transition and density changes. However, extracting latent heat information indirectly may be less straightforward.
critiques.feasibility: EML and in-situ synchrotron diagnostics are established techniques for high-temperature measurements, making the approach feasible, though it demands access to specialized facilities.
critiques.evidence: Techniques for in-situ structural and phase change observation in similar high-temperature alloy systems have been reported (e.g., PMC8320920, PMC6207727, PMC10384371, PMC11052300).
critiques.main_risk: The indirect determination of enthalpy and entropy from structural data may introduce uncertainties compared to direct calorimetric measurements.
critiques.fix: Integrate complementary calorimetric techniques or develop robust data analysis protocols to quantitatively correlate the in-situ XRD and imaging data with the latent heat and entropy changes.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the question by measuring the phase-transition thermal effects using DSC and complementary dilatometry, and it clearly specifies the targeted properties (melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change). The physical rationale is well‐established, and the experimental throughput is high due to miniaturization and automation. The main criticism concerns the challenge of integrating dilatometry accurately at high temperatures, which is fixable by implementing rigorous in‐situ calibration with high-temperature reference materials. Given the supporting evidence in prior studies and the clear quantitative performance criteria, this approach is the most straightforward and efficient for accurate determination across HEAs.
